      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Can you resize an image without any loss of quality?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "In practice, no. Any resize operation involves resampling pixels, and some information is either discarded (downscaling) or invented (upscaling). The goal is to minimize the visible loss. Downscaling from a high-quality source with a good algorithm like Bicubic or Lanczos produces results that are visually indistinguishable from the original. Upscaling always introduces some softness or artifacts, though AI upscalers can now produce convincing results for moderate size increases."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What is the best resampling algorithm for resizing photos?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "For downscaling photographs, Bicubic Sharper or Lanczos generally produce the best results by preserving edge detail and reducing softness. For upscaling by small amounts, Bicubic Smoother or Lanczos work well. For larger upscales, dedicated AI tools like Topaz Gigapixel, Upscayl, or waifu2x outperform traditional algorithms significantly. Avoid Nearest Neighbor for photographs; it is only suitable for pixel art or images that must retain hard edges without any interpolation."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "How much can I upscale an image before it looks bad?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "With traditional resampling algorithms, increases up to 150 percent typically remain acceptable for casual use. Beyond that, softness and artifacts become clearly visible. Modern AI upscalers can convincingly enlarge images by 2x to 4x, and sometimes further for specific subject types like faces or illustrations. The starting image quality matters more than the final size; a sharp 1000-pixel image upscales better than a blurry 2000-pixel image."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Should I resize before or after adding effects and borders?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Resize first, then apply effects like borders, text, or filters. Resizing after adding a border can distort the border thickness or introduce softness at the edges where crisp lines matter most. Working at the final output size means every subsequent edit is applied at the correct resolution, and text or borders remain pixel-perfect. The one exception is heavy retouching, which is easier at full resolution before the final resize."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Does resizing an image reduce its file size?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Yes. Fewer pixels means less data to store, so resizing to smaller dimensions almost always reduces file size significantly. For example, halving both dimensions of an image reduces its pixel count by 75 percent, and file size typically drops by a similar proportion. However, file size also depends on format and compression settings. Saving a resized image as PNG will produce a larger file than the same image saved as a high-quality JPEG."
        }
      }
    ]
  }
